The Administration's main defense here seems that the Council can't legislate compensation, and this is very familiar to me because I have another bill that wants to give city workers, uh, a day off if they donate an organ, and they're mounting a similar objection. And it is a little frustrating, but I'm very attuned to the argument for that reason. You argue that this legislation conflicts with the Taylor Law because compensation is a mandatory subject of bargaining. Is it your position that the City Council has no ability whatsoever to establish

compensation policies affecting municipal employees through legislation?
Uh, yes, Council Member, that is.
Are there examples where the Council has created compensation-related programs or bonuses for city employees through legislation?

Uh, there aren't that I'm aware of. I'm certainly not aware of every piece of legislation going back, but, uh, I'm not aware of it specifically. So if the Council can't legislate solutions and bargaining hasn't yet addressed the issue, what mechanism exists for addressing urgent workforce shortages like the one we're seeing with paraprofessionals?

Uh, thank you for that question. So I think, you know, you, you did say that bargaining has not yet addressed the problem, and I appreciate that because I think, you know, yet is the important part. There's always the opportunity to bargain more and to, to try to address these issues through that process. Um, I will say that, you know, we do have a closed contract with the UFT. We have an agreement going for— expiring in November of '27. That said, there have been times in the past when

we've reopened agreements in the middle to the challenges. And, you know, one thing I do wanna focus on, I obviously, I testified to the legal issues, but I, I do wanna get across that it's not just the legal issues here. I think there's a really, a practical and a fairness issue here about looking at the workforce as a whole. Because while I acknowledge the, the problems and the challenges that come from having 1,000 paraprofessional vacancies, you know, I think, and I've often, you know, testified in this Committee about vacancies in the city workforce alongside DCAS, that there are a lot of places with a lot of vacancies. Um, you know, we see, I think, some places with vacancy rates far higher than that and I think no matter what, you have to make sure that any approach you take is taken in a consistent way so that you're not treating any particular title or union or employee better than, than others. So I would say that the way to address this is to try to bargain the, the issue. Um, you know, certainly if the UFT came to us and said, we think this is a challenge that needs to be addressed now, we wanna reopen our contract. I can give you an

example. Back in 2018, I think it was, the UFT wanted to establish a paid parental leave program for their members. And, um, we reopened the contract and figured out a way to, to come to an agreement on that rather than waiting for the next agreement.

In certain schools, especially a special needs school that has a shortage of paras, it seems a lot more urgent than just a challenge. It seems by definition kind of an emergency. But you mentioned— I don't want to monopolize the questions, and I appreciate your patience— but you mentioned that OLR remains ready to work with the UFT to increase compensation. Can you tell us what specifically, what proposals the Administration has made, if any, to increase paraprofessional pay?

Uh, we have not made, uh, any proposals as of this time recently. You know, if we went back to past contract negotiations, you know, I, I would have to look to see if we made any specific proposals related to paraprofessionals during those negotiations. So if the administration believes the solution must come through collective bargaining, what's the

timeline for addressing paraprofessional compensation and the related crisis that we have with vacancies through that process?

So, you know, I, I don't think I can give a specific timeline today. I will say that the, you know, the bargaining for the next round, bargaining will have to occur at some time. Um, the contract with DC 37 expires in November of this year. Um, the UFT is later November of next year, but our contracts are starting to expire. So there certainly will come a time soon when we are engaged, kind of fully engaged in bargaining again. We're always engaged in bargaining, always ready to talk but there will come a time soon when we are in the room for a new period and I think issues like this will be front and center when we, when we get to that point.
So paraprofessionals are expected to wait until the next full bargaining cycle before seeing any relief?

Uh, I, I would say that we are willing to sit down and talk to the UFT before then about solutions. You know, it needs to be— make sure— we need to make sure it's an approach that is fair to

everyone, but we are more than willing to sit down and talk about it and see if we figure something out.

Uh, final question. So a lot of paras in this city earn barely enough to live in the communities that they serve. Do you believe the— and does the Administration believe that the current compensation structure is adequate to recruit and retain the workforce that our schools need?

Um, so I would, you know, in terms of recruitment retention of the employees, I defer to— have to defer to the Department of Education on their view of that. You know, I do - will say, you know, personally, and I've spoken about this before, there are lots of the employees that I would love to see paid more. You know, so many of the employees do incredibly valuable work, and paraprofessionals are definitely one of them. And I think in an ideal world, we would, we would pay everyone a lot more. Obviously, there are, you know, fiscal realities we have to deal with. And as I said, you have to make sure it's an approach that addresses everyone in that situation, not just, you know, one group. So, you know, I, I certainly understand the, the view. This Administration has obviously talked a lot

about affordability and, you know, their view is— the view of the Administration is clear on that. So it's an— it's a concern but like I said, any solution, we really have to look globally and make sure it doesn't, um, kind of spill over too much in a way that, that is unfair to others.
Thank you and thank you, Chair, for letting me go an extra minute.

Thank you, Council Member. Um, Council Member, um, I, I do have a couple of follow-up questions. If I may, before I turn it over to Council Member Narcisse. So, I'm done. Thank you. I'm being respectful. Um, so the, the last time this Committee discussed paraprofessionals, um, OLR stated that they're— that you were not aware of attrition analysis that was undertaken for paraprofessionals and are there plans to undertake this analysis?

Um, I believe that, um, in the last— thank you, Chair, for the question. Um, I believe that in the last hearing, um, the Department of Education had testified regarding attrition rates, that their retention rates were around 95%. Um, I, I'd have to review the testimony, but, uh, the DOE

would be the one doing any attrition analysis. I can certainly follow up and see if they have those numbers available to provide to the Committee.

And I have a follow-up, uh, follow-up on, on the comment you made about reopening the contract. Are there provisions in the current collective bargaining agreements with DC 37 or UFP that allows for a reopen-er to discuss, uh, any of the, the job titles?

Uh, there are not any explicit provisions, but, um, in the past that has not prevented OLR from, you know, agreeing to, to do so. Obviously we can agree to whatever we want to agree to. So, um, in the past, OLR has reopened contracts even that did not have explicit reopen or provisions to talk about kind of challenges, including working out with the UFT a paid parental leave program.

So what has been the barrier to, um, uh, negotiating better compensation for this group of, uh, of job titles or this group of workers that are clearly - it feels like we're at a crisis point with the number of vacancies that's only gonna

grow because of the need, um, coming with the expansion of 3K, uh, the 3K program.

Um, you know, I, I don't think I'd say that there's something preventing it. I think that, you know, we have not received a request from the UFT. We normally do not, um, start, you know, engaging in bargaining if a union doesn't, especially midterm, if a union doesn't indicate a desire to do so. They have not come to us and asked to bargain. They've, they've only kind of come forth with, with this legislation. We have not, uh, we have not gotten any kind of requests from them to, to discuss this issue.

Okay. Um, and, um, so when OLR negotiates with the, with the bargaining representative, um, that represents multiple, you know, job titles, um, like UFT, for example, um, do you consider the negotiations, uh, for each civil service title independently, or is everyone subject to just the same, uh, pattern?

Uh, so our approach, you know, as I said, we try to be flexible. So, you know, under the pattern bargaining approach that the city, you

know, engages in, typically what we look at is the total cost of an agreement for a bargaining unit. So, you know, in the case of some unions, it's very small. We have 100-person bargaining units, we have 3-person bargaining units, and then we're just looking at that title. If you only represent one title, we, we look at one title but for a union like the UFT or DC37, we look at kind of the cost of the whole agreement. And if a union wants to put more money towards one title, then we will look at that. We'll look at the total cost and kind of evaluate it in a global context. We won't say, No, you can't give more to one title than to another. That's not something we would, we would say to a union. We would certainly want to discuss it, discuss the reasons for focusing on one title rather than another, but we have done so in the past and would continue to do so.
Okay. Um, Council Member Narcisse, you had a question?

Oh yes, I do. Okay. Um, I was following the— hmm, mhm, like, you know, I mean. Thank you, Chair. Thank you for the opportunity to speak and ask some questions.

Um, I have a lot of writing here, but I have to get to the point, that's not my hearing. But I want to say, historically, how has paraprofessional pay in New York City changed over the past 10, 20 years, and has it kept, I mean, pace with the rising cost of living in the city?

Uh, thank you for the question, Council Member. Um, I, you know, to do a full analysis, I would have to get back to you but, you know, in the past, it would vary depending on whether you're looking at 10, 20 years. Um, the last 10 years, I think wage increases have generally been somewhere around 2.5, 3%. Um, I think if you look at the, the probably past couple decades and you looked at the, you know, wage increases employees have generally received versus inflation, you'd find that in low inflation periods, they tend to— it's the wages tend to exceed inflation. In, in high inflation periods, they, they tend to be a bit lower, but I don't have a kind of across some time period analysis right now I can speak to.
Is the Administration tracking how many paraprofessionals leave the system each year due to the wages?

Uh, so I would have to, to confer with the Department of Education to get that information. I know they do obviously track who leaves. I don't know if they have any kind of exit interview process set up where they are able to, um, kind of assign a reason?

Uh, for many reasons, I'm reading, I'm reading from your quote here. Both the city and the, and its unions must have confidence that when an agreement is reached, its terms will govern. If compensation changes could instead be enacted through legislation outside of the process, Why make a deal at all? This is interesting to me because when the paraprofessional cannot pay the bill, knowing the rising cost and all this. So now if they're coming to us, and if I'm correct, uh, from what you said, now if we cannot pass any bill to change that, their children, their home, what they eat, have to wait? How do we do it?

So I, I completely appreciate the, the question and the sentiment and the, the thought behind that. And, you know, as I said, I think there are ways that we could have the discussion through

the bargaining process where this should be. Um, but, you know, the other thing I just say is that we, we need to be conscious of everyone because they are not, you know, they're not the lowest paid. They, they, they're not the lowest paid employees in the city necessarily. There are a lot of other employees who, who make similar wages and, you know, whatever we end up doing, you know, whatever approach we would take, I think we want to be sure that we're fair to every city worker. So that was, you know, when OLR talks about pattern bargaining, and I know a lot of people question it, a lot of people say this seems overly rigid. Um, for us, it really is about making sure that we're thinking of the, the whole picture about every union, every employee, and that we're not, you know, just taking one group at a time and maybe, you know, treating them differently than everyone else. So, you know, I understand the sentiment. I, I wish I had an answer that said we could give $10,000 to every city employee. Um, but, you know, as you know, we, we have fiscal constraints as well, so.

To me, it's more than sentiment. This is people's lives. And this is what

they eat and as a healthcare professional, that's their health. Many schools struggle to recruit paraprofessionals because the pay does not reflect the responsibilities of the job. Do you believe this payment will make the profession more suitable to help bring more qualified candidates into the system?

So I'm not the best person to speak about kind of the recruitment of paraprofessionals. You know, I, I will say obviously, you know, offering more money helps recruit —It's not, uh, you know, generally speaking, that helps. It doesn't always— it's not always a magic bullet. Some jobs, there are challenges beyond money that, um, that, that impact recruitment and I think there are always other strategies you can look at that aren't just money, but I'm not gonna sit here and tell you that, like, adding $10,000 wouldn't make a difference and I wouldn't say that. Um, but, you know, I, I would have to ultimately on, on all the nuances have to defer to

Hmm. You cannot say it, and I cannot say it either because those are the people that educating our kids every single day, more

than even sometimes the teachers. Their hands overwhelmed, and we know that and I don't want to beat on you, but I'm just saying my job is to listen to them and coming to a solution, because there's a problem in the house right now. It's education for our children. They're educating our kids. They're helping us to build the future that we all talk about. Um, You talk about— I'm about to finish Chair. Uh, you will sit down. I mean, if I quote you correctly, you want to sit down, right? So to listen, to see how— because based on the question of my colleagues, but how long they've been crying, saying that this is not working and they're asking for help. So you never had a chance to really dive into it to see how the best way you can help?

Um, I wouldn't say that. I would say that, you know, we have— we negotiate agreements with the UFT and other unions. Those negotiations are lengthy, and ultimately we come to an agreement that, that both parties, you know, decide to put out to their— that decide to live by, that the city agrees to, that the union agrees to put out to their

membership, that the membership ultimately ratifies. And sometimes you can't address everything. Sometimes maybe an issue wasn't raised as prominently as it, as it should have been. Sometimes maybe the issue wasn't as prominent when we were sitting down as it has become after that. And so that's why either, you know, when that happens, you can either come sit down, try to find a way to, to reopen bargaining and see if that works for both parties, because ultimately it has to work for both. Um, or you can wait until your contract expires. I think those are really the, but, but it always should be through that process is my view, because truth is there are always, you know, there are two parties in it, right? So the fact that this was— there was not anything in an agreement, you know, that was related specific to paraprofessionals. It wasn't just OLR's agreement. It was an OLR and UFT agreement and any, I think, any effort to, to change that and to go back and change that should involve both parties discussing it as we so frequently do.

It is difficult, and I'm gonna stop right here. This is not my hearing, but

their bills cannot wait, their children cannot wait. And, uh, I understand the bargaining, I understand all that. This have to take place. But in the meanwhile, you cannot tell someone that cannot pay the bills to wait. If they wait, they have to wait for a purpose, and a good one too. So I hope they get that extra. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chair.
Council— thank you, Council Member Narcisse. Uh, uh, Council Member De La Rosa.

Thank you, Chair, and good to see you again. Um, look, I think as the former Chair of this Committee, I, I think that my colleagues and I perfectly understand the importance of collective bargaining as the cornerstone of unionized work. Um, and we also understand the bounds of the laws when it comes to the jurisdiction of the Council, but the question I have for you; do you know how much the city pays in, um, Carter cases a year?
Uh, those are not numbers I have at hand. Um, I know it's, it's very significant.

$1 billion annually. And would you agree with me that the city's legally

mandated to provide special education, um, to children who need it?
Um, so, you know, I'm certainly not an expert in that area, but that's my understanding.

It is. They are legally mandated and so, you know, here what we have is the picking and choosing of how we, um, apply law because if we have a legal mandate to provide special education supports to children and we're spending $1 billion annually, then there is both a legal argument and a fiscal argument as to why this legislation makes sense. And I understand that in collective bargaining, you all will get into the details of how that happens and and where compensation structures happen. But I would argue that in this moment, when we have a legal mandate to provide services for families, we can't wait because this is a workforce that is in crisis. I will— I would be the first one. I think all of us here, I can— I can't speak for all of us, but I think I have a, a good sense that all of us here, I've seen all of these ladies at picket lines very recently for the nurses, would all stand in favor of ensuring that

workers across this city are fairly paid and that, that, then that, that negotiation is done in a fair and comprehensive way and I understand how the pattern works. But you have a situation with the paras where that pattern is creating and growing a crisis for a workforce that is necessary inside our schools right now. And so the Council is attempting with this law to try and mitigate that crisis before it balloons out of control, because it's costing us $1 billion annually. The fiscal impact statement for this legislation is $400 million. So there's a cost savings there and in a time where we have a gap to close, I would think I, and I'm not saying that all of the $1 billion would be closed by this particular bill, but I think it would make a dent in the type of supports that, uh, the most vulnerable students in our city need. Um, and so I wanna speak to that. I wish that the DOE was here. I'm not gonna, um, lie and, and, and I wish that they were here to answer some of the questions. I understand that they couldn't be here today, but, uh, as we navigate the vacancy rates across the city for agencies, I was glad to hear, um,

that this Administration is looking at policies like the 2-for-1 hire, which have created ballooning vacancies in agencies. And so I think we can walk and chew gum at the same time. We can tackle vacancies by changing policies that are not working, like the 2-for-1 hire rule, and pass legislation to make sure that we're keeping with our legal mandate. Um, and then I, I don't know if you have the, the authority to speak to this, but it is my understanding that as a candidate, the Mayor supported paraprofessionals. Um, do you have reason to believe, um, that Mayor Mamdani would support this type of legislation?

Um, so I can't speak specifically to that. Um, I will say that, you know, from, from our perspective, it's not a matter of, um, or from OLR's perspective, you know, it's not a matter of saying, you know, we're not sitting here saying, oh, you know, we don't think that— we think the pay is perfectly fine where it is, there's no problem whatsoever, like, we don't you know, this shouldn't be an issue. I think we're just saying that it has to be addressed in a more global way and through the, the

kind of process that it's supposed to be addressed through. Um, you know, there obviously are the, the fiscal realities we face. Obviously the Mayor's talked about those realities and, you know, whatever you do, obviously you talked about the $400 million impact of this bill, which isn't insignificant. Um, and then, you know, beyond that, there's what would come next for other titles if, this, uh, this troop got something like, like that. So it wouldn't be limited, I think, to 400 million. So ultimately, you know, it's about balancing those realities but I think, you know, we are interested in, in, you know, making sure that whatever we do going forward in bargaining, that we're looking at issues like this. I will say in the last round of bargaining, you know, we, we tried to, to some degree, focus on recruitment and retention issues because when we were engaged in bargaining back in 2023, I know Council Member De La Rosa, you called a lot of attention to this. There were a lot of recruitment retention challenges. There still are. I think we've made a lot of efforts to, to try to, um, not, you know, certainly eliminate those issues, but try to help with those issues.

We did things like equity funding. We did things like that, that, um, were kind of efforts to, to enhance our ability to get people and they may not have been perfect. They may not have solved the problem permanently but I think as we look towards new bargaining, whether it's the next round or a union's desire to reopen a contract, you know, and, and, and talk more, we would be focused on that issue then as well.

Well, we're looking forward to obviously working with OLR. I think that it is important to note that, um, this Administration, this Council, all of us have been laser-focused on affordability. I can think of no other way to make the city more affordable than to pay people the wages that they deserve. These unionized workers, these essential workers of our city. I have a, a child in the New York City Public School system. I see the work that they do every single day to make sure that our children are safe and educated and as the Chair noted, with the expansion of programs like 2K and 3K, um, we're gonna need more of them, not just to meet that 1,044

vacancy, but we need to expand this workforce and we can attract them. I mean, $30,000 a year when someone is paying $2,000 rent a month. I mean, you can, you can qualify for food stamps with that, with that wage and so, we have to take into account that these are real human beings doing real important work, and that we all need to collectively come together to find the solution. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member De La Rosa. Um, I do have a— I mean, I do have a question. I— it's actually more of a comment. Um, you know, I worked in labor for many years, public sector and private sector. Um, and I understand, you know, that pattern bargaining is meant to kind of make a level playing field, but that doesn't work when you have such structural pay disparities that are based on a number of issues. Could be gender bias, racial bias, uhm, and I, I see, you know, jobs like these that are you know, largely women, uh, women of color, uh, nothing against the men out there, but the, the reality is that there's a structural bias built into, uh, you know, the wages that are paid to, uh, certain groups

of workers, and the pattern bargaining does not fix that. Um, my other comment is that, you know, the UFT has come to the City Council to try to alleviate this problem. To me, it seems like they had no other recourse but to come to the City Council because they had— they, they were unable to reopen bargaining to, uh, deal with this particular issue. So, um, yeah.

Thank you, um, Chair Aldebol and that, you know, I, I do want to say, obviously you know, the— this Administration has not engaged in a, you know, round of collective bargaining yet. Obviously, when— as we do bargaining, every administration has different priorities. And, you know, certainly this administration, I think, should have an opportunity to engage in that process with an eye towards some of— some of their priorities, which I think are, you know, many of those that— that, uh, too many have spoken to. Um, so I think there— there are opportunities. I think there are opportunities for a pattern to kind of recognize those realities and try to deal with them. Um, you know, not saying that every pattern

that we've had did that. There are some— maybe some patterns didn't do enough. We have been making an effort in recent ones to, to set aside funding for uses like this. Um, and, you know, I think we look forward to trying to continue to look at how we can, you know, within the, the constructs that we have, within the— in a way that's fair to everyone, how we can, you know, try to deal with situations like the one the Council is paying attention to.

So, and based on, on your testimony today, are you saying that— and, and also based on, you know, the Mayor's commitment to, uh, raise wages, uh, for this group of workers and others, uh, are you saying that, uh, the city OLR would, if UFT were to approach you or DC 37 were to approach you you about reopening the contract to increase compensation for this group of workers, that you would, uh, agree to do so?

Um, you know, I'm not able to, to make a commitment about formally reopening. I will say we'll always have a discussion. You know, we've, we've done it in the past, and if they came to us and said that, we would, we would have the discussion

about what the possibilities are and whether we're willing to do that. We're always, we're always willing to talk. We're always willing to sit down, listen. We, we're not— we don't normally just say you have a closed contract, you know, go away. We're always willing to talk.
Thank you. Um, uh, welcome, Council Member, uh, Cabán. Do you have any questions? No? Okay, thank you. Thank you for your testimony.
Thank you.

So, okay, so I, I I'm now going to open the floor for, uh, to public testimony. Before we begin, I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding, that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance— an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait for your name to be called. Once you have been recognized, you will have 2 minutes to speak on today's legislation, Intro 692. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that to the Sergeant-at-Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. When you hear your name, please come up to the witness panel. I see— it's amazing— President Michael Mulgrew is already here. He said, I'm ready. Uh, I would, uh, call up Vice Chair Anthony Barnes, uh, Michelle Herman, Policy Director for UFT, John Camp— John, John Camps, Vice Chair for paras— paraprofessionals, and Chapter Chairperson also for UFT, uh, Priscilla Castro. Good, got everybody. Where's Priscilla? Hey, Priscilla. Okay, okay, we're waiting for— I hear Bridget, I hear Bridget directing people behind me. Um, okay, thank you.

Okay, thank you so much. Uh, thank you, Chair, and, uh, we do appreciate you having this hearing. We're very happy at this first hearing. So thank you so much, uh, especially on this important issue. Um, we are submitting testimony, and I just want you to know that we also are submitting over 50 testimonials from paraprofessionals who are all working right now inside of schools. After listening to OLR's responses, you know, I'm getting a little disgusted with this whole thing, and I appreciate the questions from City Council. They're fact— they're that they continue to sit back and say it's an, uh, it's a subject of collective bargaining. I want to be clear and make sure that you and everyone in public understands their position inside of a collective bargaining venue is that other workers must pay for this, not the city. And that is why this is getting more and more, in what I'm concerning, to be very, very ugly because the reality is we are short thousands of paraprofessionals. Every one of those paraprofessionals that we are short is a crisis for a family and a child. Is the off of— Office of Labor Relations of New York City— what is their job? Is their job to go

after workers and try to make other workers pay for their mistakes, or is their job to try to staff the City of New York's agencies properly for them to deliver the services that are required? And when it comes to children, the fact that they continue to hold to this ridiculous argument— and it is only an argument, it is not a law, it is not a regulation, it is not a requirement. The city can do this. It is OLR and OMB's position to continue to cause great pain to children and their families, and they hide behind something that is completely untrue. There is nothing that says the City of New York must adhere to this pattern of saying other workers need to pay for the raises. You cannot hire the people you need to do the job. Let's just start with simple things. The, the cost of living in New York City, and that a paraprofessional starts at $30,000. A paraprofessional in Boston is— starts at $41,000, and their cost of living is much less. So we appreciate this hearing, and again, we thank you for introducing this bill, and we just say enough is enough and I think we should do a hearing about what is the actual job of OLR of New York City.
Thank you. Um, next.

Good afternoon. Thank you, Chair. My name is Priscilla Castro. I'm the Chairperson for the paraprofessionals in New York City, all 26,000. No, no, it's okay. Um, thank you, uh, Carmen De La Rosa for introducing this bill. This respect check means a lot for all the paraprofessionals in New York City. Collective bargaining does not work. The 3%, 4% that we have been enduring all these years in collective bargaining is a disgrace. $33,000? Our paraprofessionals cannot survive. Our students need our paraprofessionals. The paraprofessionals are the backbone of the classroom. It's not right. We talk about 1,000 paraprofessionals. It's way more than that. 3,000 to 4,000 paraprofessionals needed. These are students without services, students with disabilities that need paraprofessionals. And every day we are losing paraprofessionals. Why? Because of the wage. Not because they want to leave the profession. They have to leave the profession. Who can live on $33,000? They cannot live in New York City, so they're leaving New York City, and it's not right,

and we have to do something about that, and this legislation will do just that. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good evening. Did I just turn it on? Is it on? So good evening. Thank you for this opportunity. My name is Anthony Barnes, and I am the Assistant Secretary of the UFT Paraprofessional Chapter. Um, almost 33 years ago, I was a subparaprofessional, and the problems that I saw then are still here, right? Um, imagine getting a check and you still can't meet your bills. Imagine having your lights turned off. Imagine being homeless. And these are paraprofessionals that we talk to on a daily basis as we visit schools and we meet these members. And not only do we have shortages, but there are paraprofessionals that are expected to do the job of 2 and 3 paraprofessionals in the school, and they're punished if they don't do it.
